title: Dino Polska H1’2026 Update
content_html:
Dear Partners,

The Polish supermarket chain Dino Polska reported its half-year results for 2026 last week, and the share price rose by 8 per cent on the results. After reading the financial results and the call in my opinion, underlying performance remains quite strong despite macroeconomic headwinds and an ongoing price war in Poland. I’ll take you through the developments.

Dino Polska store concept

I’ll give you a quick breakdown on the business Dino Polska. Dino’s store concept is a combination of a discount supermarket and a convenience store, where the ‘convenience’ comes from the fact that the supermarkets are located close to the customer.

“DINO – CLOSEST TO YOU”

Dino operates a standardised, universal store model and stocks a range of 5,000 different products (SKUs). In terms of floor area, at 400 m², they are much smaller than rival discounters such as Biedronka or Lidl (which are often around 1,000+ m²).

Unlike its competitors, Dino has built all its stores itself and generates its own electricity using solar panels. Something else that competitors of Dino not have is that every Dino supermarket has its own in-store butcher (supplied with meat that Dino produces itself through a subsidiary).

Share

Total Stores

Personally I like the story of how a supermarket chain could grow so fast in areas where there was little or no competition, with no additional funding since IPO and no debt. Founder/CEO Biernacki saw the opportunity that customers had to drive kilometres to get their grocerries and went all-in.

In the first half-year of 2026, Dino expanded the chain to 3,176 stores. In 2016 Dino had just 628 stores. A 5x in less than ten years. Remarkable

For me, whether Dino will be a good investment depends on the prospects regarding the number of stores the company can still open. And secondly: how long can this growth be sustained, at what ROIIC, before cannibalisation sets in?

A Dino store serves a region with 2,500–3,500 inhabitants.There is still plenty of room for growth if they manage to increase the number of stores to 15 per 100,000 across the country. My estimations are that there is +/- room for a total of 5,700 Dino stores in Poland based on the regional coverage. That is almost an 1.8x increase from the current 3,176 stores.

Whilst Dino has been able to grow in smaller towns for many years, competition for Dino is certainly intensifying. Its competitor and Poland’s largest supermarket chain, Biedronka, is mainly present in the major cities, but is now also opening more new supermarkets in smaller towns.

“Usually the sales density is a little bit lower, but also the cost structure is and the rents, et cetera, are also low. In fact, you don’t see, you know, a big difference in terms of return on invested capital on these smaller stores.”

“I would say that probably it [gross margin] may be a little bit lower depending on the categories, but again, the costs are also different. I would say that the way that we look at it is that from a profitability point of view, it doesn’t dilute or differ much from the rest, from the urban ones.”

“On the expansion plan in Poland, what we see is still some white spaces in Poland. We think that instead of having just our competitors opening in the locations, we feel that not only it makes sense to have a Biedronka store as we will grab part of the market, we will continue to open. We think that expansion for now, as we flag, will continue to be a driver for growth.” - Jerónimo Martins, H1 2026 Earnings Call

Revenue

In H1’26, Dino’s revenue grew by 12.5 per cent. This growth in revenue is driven by the opening of new stores and growth from existing Dino stores. Over the past three years, Dino has opened more than 300 stores annually, and currently around 25 per cent to 30 per cent of its total network is in the non-mature phase (less than 36 months old). This year aloneDino will open around 380 to 395 stores.

A new Dino store reaches full maturity after approximately 3 years (around 36 months). These newly opened stores have not yet reached their full revenue and profit potential, whilst fixed costs are already putting immediate pressure on profits. You see this back in lower margins.

Like for Like Sales

Next to growth from opening new stores, revenue growth is partly driven by growth from existing stores (like-for-like). This type og growth is for me one of the most important KPIs to monitor. At the time of my purchase two years ago, Dino was consistently outperforming Polish food inflation and its competitors here. In recent quarters, the company does not performing as well as did before.

The low LFL growth is caused by a combination of macroeconomic factors and changing consumer behaviour; Let me break those down.

Basket deflation: Purchase prrices for agricultural commodities (such as pork, dairy, cereals and poultry) have fallen sharply. And partly due to the ongoing price war, supermarkets in Poland are forced to pass on these falling prices directly to consumers in the form of lower prices. This results in basket deflation at the checkout.

Price war: Discounters such as Biedronka and Lidl have been locked in a nationwide battle for some time now, using substantial promotions and discounts on products to gain market share. This price war has been putting pressure on LFL for some time.

“Sales grew 1.7% to EUR 12.6 billion or 1.9% in local currency, with like-for-like up 0.2% despite significant basket deflation. H1 volumes rose by around 5%, offsetting the impact of like-for-like from deflation and preserving our main banner’s market share. Deflation accelerated markedly in Q2, resulting in sales slightly below Q2 ‘25 and in a like-for-like of minus 1.6%, while like-for-like volumes grew by more than 4%.”- Ana Luisa Virgínia (CFO Jerónimo Martins), H1 2026 Earnings Call

“Looking ahead, we continue to see persistent basket deflation and consumer caution across Poland through the third quarter with no immediate turning point. Biedronka will continue prioritizing volume-led growth and price competitiveness over aggressive margin expansion.” - Ana Luisa Virgínia (CFO Jerónimo Martins), H1 2026 Earnings Call

Cautious consumers: In recent years, customers have seen their purchasing power decline due to high inflation. They simply had/have less money available each month for groceries. As a result, consumers are on the lookout for good deals. Today, consumers are finding some breathing space again thanks to minimum wage rises in Poland.

“I can say once again that what we are focusing on is delivering volumes. That is our number one goal, our top goal.” - Michał Krauze (CFO Dino Polska), H1’2026 Earnings Call

Why I’m still optimistic despite a lower LFL; Despite macroeconomic headwinds and a price war, Dino managed to achieve real volume growth of 6 per cent from existing stores in the first half of the year, compared with 5 per cent for Biedronka. Total volume growth stood at 16.3 per cent, compared with 6.9 per cent for Biedronka.

Profitablity

There are currently a number of factors that are putting significant pressure on margins. The growth in volume is not only leading to busier checkouts, but is also increasing the workload across the entire Dino chain. In addition, Dino opened 148 new stores in the first half of the year. This resulted in 5,000 new employees in the first half of the year.

Dino’s workforce grew by 12.8 per cent year-on-year, whilst the minimum wage in Poland rose by 14.5 per cent over the same period. This explains the pressure on margins,tight labour market and the ongoing price war is not helping margins improve either.

In overall terms, Dino is still substantially smaller than Biedronka or Lidl. The downside of this price war is that Dino is still a long way from having the same economies of scale as Biedronka or Lidl. These competitors relies on a much higher proportion of own-brand (private label) products, whilst Dino mainly sells premium brands.

The problem in my opnion with selling premium brands, from manufacturers such as Unilever. Is that these manufactures largely determine the purchasing terms and margins, meaning that Dino’s purchasing advantage is more limited than with private label purchasing. I think in the long term, this presents an opportunity for Dino, but in the short term, this is one reason next to their lower economies of scale why Dino is at a disadvantage compared to the competition.

Valuation

At the time of my purchase, I made an mistake in my analysis regarding the valuation and competitive position. Prior to my purchase, Dino was able to pass on price increases to customers due to high inflation, which led to a period of strong growth in like-for-like sales. This growth generated a form of operational leverage, resulting in higher margins. I should have asked myself better questions and, above all, inverted the positive aspects I saw at the time of purchase.

  • Am I paying a high growth multiple on structurally sustainable profits or on cyclically inflated profits? How much of the +10% LFL growth is genuine organic demand; was the strong ‘operating leverage’ an inflationary tailwind?

  • Does the operational cost structure work just as much against the business in a more challenging period as it did in favour of it when Dino had the wind in its sails?

  • At the time, I believed that Dino was the cost leader, but was that actually the case on this scale when it had a 10 per cent market share, without private-label products?

  • Is Dino so deeply ingrained in customers’ shopping habits that the ‘low advertising costs’ represent a structural moat or a temporary windfall due to underpenetration? And is the staffed meat counter a scalable competitive advantage or a labour-intensive pitfall, carrying extreme risks?

I do not yet have answers to some of these questions, and I will use the coming period to reflect on them further. Still, the question stays the same: how long can Dino keep growing, and at what ROIIC? My expectations are based entirely on the statements made by management, namely that they will be fully focused on expanding the chain. This means that, in terms of capital allocation, almost all operating cash flows will be used for expansion Capex in the coming years.

Following a phase of growth, Dino will enter a phase of maturity. During this phase, Dino will spend less on expansion Capex. Dino has no debt, and part of the maintenance costs is already factored into the P&L. This means that a significant amount of cash flows can be returned to shareholders via dividends and share buy-backs.

Corporate Governance

Management tells us very little, and the founder/CEO Biernacki has more or less vanished from public view. That makes it hard to estimate their long-term plans. Sometimes I get the feeling management would rather not be listed at all. The IPO happened, because a private equity firm wanted to sell its stake, and going public let Biernacki keep full control.

“The listing was never really about raising money”

After years of expansion, Biernacki could decide in the futher to take the company private again. If he does than I hope that Biernacki will use the fcf to buy back and cancel shares over time, so the ones who stay own more of a bigger business.

Conclusion Casteleyn Partnership

Due to my own mistakes, I had projected a more positive picture of Dino’s future. currently, Dino is facing macroeconomic headwinds, but the underlying business is performing well despite these headwinds.

Dino is my smallest position in the portfolio; although I have been a shareholder for two years, it accounts for only 2.75 per cent of the portfolio and I have never felt strongly enough to expand the holding further. Nevertheless, Dino is in my opninion a company where you’re unlikely to lose your money and a business that will still be around in 10–20 years’ time.

I’ll be taking some time in the coming period to think carefully about the company and the position in my portfolio, as I do have a number of companies in the portfolio where I do have conviction and also offering more attractive IRRs than Dino Polska.

‘‘Patient capital. Driven by the discipline of learning.’’ - Casteleyn Partnership
